bio.en: Inbal Shani is a product executive who served as Chief Product Officer of Ironclad and is now Chief Product Officer at LinkedIn, where she leads development of the world's largest professional network.
bio.zh: Inbal Shani 是一位产品高管，曾担任 Ironclad 的首席产品官，现任 LinkedIn 首席产品官，领导全球最大职业社交网络的开发。

summary.en: In this conversation, Inbal draws on her experience leading product at high-scale companies to share hard-won lessons on what it takes to build and lead great product organizations. She discusses how product leaders can earn trust, scale decision-making, and grow both their teams and their own careers. The episode is full of practical wisdom for product managers and leaders who want to operate at the highest level.
summary.zh: 在这期对话中，Inbal 结合在大型公司领导产品的经验，分享了打造并领导卓越产品组织的来之不易的教训。她谈到产品领导者如何赢得信任、放大决策规模，以及如何让团队与自己一同成长。这期节目充满面向想在高层面运作的 PM 与领导者的实用智慧。

turns.speaker: Inbal Shani
turns.en: The user of the AI tools to develop software needs to form a different thinking. You need to start figuring out how are you using these AI tools to help you be successful. And it's no longer just the actual code writing, it's really evolving your thinking to the big picture, to the connected experience, to connected systems, which today we just find it more in the world of more senior developers and less and less in the junior developers. (00:24): The junior developers, when they start, usually we expect them to be able to write simple code. But if now there is an AI system that is helping them writing code, they can spend more time from the get-go understanding the system, understanding the environment that they're building, or understanding that product that they're building, which today they don't have time because they're still learning how to code.
turns.zh: 使用人工智能工具开发软件的用户需要形成一种不同的思维模式。你需要开始思考如何利用这些人工智能工具助力自己取得成功。这不再仅仅是编写代码的问题，而是要将思维提升到更宏观的层面——关注整体架构、互联体验以及系统协同。如今，这种思维模式更多地存在于资深开发者群体中，而在初级开发者中则越来越少见。（00:24）对于初级开发者而言，他们入行时通常被要求能编写简单的代码。但如果现在有AI系统能帮助他们编写代码，他们就能从一开始就投入更多时间去理解系统、熟悉构建环境或深入理解所开发的产品。然而如今，他们往往没有这样的时间，因为他们仍在学习编程基础知识。

turns.speaker: Inbal Shani
turns.en: Awesome. Thank you for having me. I'm excited to be here.
turns.zh: 太棒了。感谢邀请我。我很高兴能来这里。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to start with just a broad question about where software development is going. It feels like you're at the center of the storm of what is changing in software development. It almost feels like GitHub kicked off the storm with the launch of Copilot. So let me ask, what do you think is overhyped in terms of what is changing in software development and then what do you think is underhyped?
turns.zh: 首先，我想谈一个关于软件开发发展方向的宏观问题。感觉你正处于软件开发变革风暴的中心。GitHub推出了Copilot功能，几乎引发了这场风暴。那么，我想问一下，在你看来，软件开发领域有哪些被过度炒作的趋势，又有哪些被低估的趋势？

turns.speaker: Inbal Shani
turns.en: So I joined GitHub as a CPO basically a year ago. Two days ago, I celebrated my first year. And for me, the initial approach is let's look at the platform, let's look at the software development lifecycle, and draw some conviction. And for me, the biggest conviction is that developer happiness and productivity strongly depends on their environment and dev tooling. And as such, AI is really critical to that mission. (05:11): When we're looking into what's happening right now with AI, it really became table stakes on expectations among developers, and it's really central and critical for them to be able to do their job. We know that something like 92% of developers are already using AI tools. But in that landscape, some of the things that are overhyped is that generative AI will replace humans. I don't see that happening in the near future. The way I think about it, you always need that human in the loop because AI cannot replace innovation. (05:45): That creative spark, that creative thinking that is the center of humanity, this will not be replaced by AI, at least not in the near future. If we think about what does that mean having an AI tool that is successful, you need data. In order to generate data, you need humans using tools, acting with tools, doing something, something. So I think the overhype that is happening right now is that generative AI will replace humanity. It's going to be the solution for everything, and I think it's a tool. (06:15): If I'm drilling down to the things that are underhyped right now in the world of software development, I'm starting hearing a little bit more on AI driven testing, but there's not lots of mention on it. And if we're thinking about the world of AI where we're going to generate much code, much more productive, much more efficient, more lines of code, more application, then testing is becoming such a critical part of that journey of developing software. (06:43): And I would like to hear more about that and what companies are thinking about how do they use AI to generate a larger suite of testing to be able to validate the work.
turns.zh: 大约一年前，我加入GitHub担任首席产品官。两天前，我庆祝了加入一周年。对我来说，最初的思路是先审视平台，研究软件开发生命周期，并形成一些坚定的信念。对我来说，最重要的信念是开发者的幸福感和生产力高度依赖于他们的环境和开发工具。因此，人工智能对实现这一目标至关重要。（05:11）：当我们审视当前人工智能的发展趋势时，它已成为开发者期望的基本要求，对他们完成工作至关重要。我们知道，已有92%的开发者在使用人工智能工具。但在这一领域，一些被过度炒作的观点是生成式人工智能将取代人类。我认为这在短期内不太可能实现。在我看来，人类始终是必不可少的环节，因为人工智能无法替代创新。（05:45）：人类的创造力和创造性思维是人类的核心所在，至少在短期内不会被人工智能取代。如果我们思考一个成功的人工智能工具意味着什么，我们需要数据。为了生成数据，我们需要人类使用工具、操作工具、完成实际操作。因此，我认为当前被过度炒作的观点是生成式人工智能将取代人类。人们认为它能解决一切问题，但它只是一种工具。（06:15）：如果深入探讨软件开发领域目前被低估的趋势，我注意到关于人工智能驱动测试的讨论越来越多，但相关提及并不多。考虑到未来我们将生成更多代码、提高生产力和效率、编写更多代码行、开发更多应用的AI世界，测试将成为软件开发过程中至关重要的一环。（06:43）：我希望能听到更多关于这一领域的讨论，以及各公司如何利用人工智能生成更全面的测试套件来验证工作成果。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And by testing you mean like unit testing, integration testing, things like that?
turns.zh: 你说的测试是指单元测试、集成测试之类的吗？

turns.speaker: Inbal Shani
turns.en: All of them, load testing, load testing, infrastructure testing, security testing, penetration testing. When you need a human to write all these testing capabilities, you need a lot of humans that needs to form different thinking. Can we leverage AI to really generate that testing suite that test everything that you need from unit testing and functional testing to load testing, to performance testing? (07:23): There's a lot of testing that we do that we don't even consider them as testing, so we don't necessarily spend a lot of time in doing them. But if we're now saying software is in the center of everything, all companies will become a software company in some form or another, there is more code being generated. Hence, the importance of testing is becoming much more critical.
turns.zh: 它们包括负载测试、负载测试、基础设施测试、安全测试、渗透测试。当你需要人工编写所有这些测试用例时，就需要大量具备不同思维方式的人才。能否借助人工智能真正生成一套测试套件，涵盖从单元测试、功能测试到负载测试、性能测试等所有需求？（07:23）：我们进行的许多测试甚至不被视为真正的测试，因此我们往往不愿投入大量时间进行这些测试。但既然我们现在说软件是万物之源，所有公司都将以某种形式成为软件公司，代码生成量也随之增加，因此测试的重要性正变得愈发关键。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's follow that thread. You talked about how you don't see software engineers completely disappearing. What's your just general sense of how software development will be different in three to five years? What do you think is going to be different? And then also just how do you see the end state of all of this of Copilot and tools like this getting better and better and better? What do you think this ends?
turns.zh: 让我们继续探讨这个话题。你提到你认为软件工程师不会完全消失。那么你对未来三到五年软件开发会发生哪些变化有什么总体看法？你认为会有哪些不同之处？另外，对于Copilot和类似工具不断改进并最终达到更高水平，你如何看待这一趋势的终极形态？你认为这一趋势会如何收束？

turns.speaker: Inbal Shani
turns.en: For me, and I keep on saying that again and again, Copilot is a copilot. It's not a pilot. You still need the human in the loop. But that means that now the software developer or the user of the AI tools to develop software needs to form a different thinking. One, you need to start thinking more systems, more architecture. You need to start figuring out how are you using these AI tools to help you be successful? And it's no longer just the actual code writing, it's really evolving your thinking to the big picture, to the connected experience, to connected systems. (08:36): And what we will see in the fullness of time that developers, one, will adopt much more of that mindset, which today we find it in software development, don't get me wrong, we just find it more in the world of more senior developers and less and less in the junior developers. The junior developers, when they start, usually we expect them to be able to write simple code. (08:57): But if now there is an AI assistant that is helping them writing code, they can spend more time from the get-go understanding the system and understanding the environment that they're building or understanding the product that they're building, which today they don't have time because they are still learning how to code. So I think that's one element. The second element that I expect to see changes is in the world of hardware development, because we know that AI has a big footprint and requires a lot of resources. (09:24): And in order to be able to meet the scale, to meet the demand, we need to be able to improve our hardware, our CPUs, our GPUs, our compute and optimization of code. And that's another area that today it's a niche of people that are spending time and I think it'll become much more aligned across the software development lifecycle. (09:44): Integration with AI is something that will definitely become something that is more normal for every developer, is today something that we start seeing that revolution, that acceptance, that AI tools, I need to figure out how to integrate with AI, I need to know how to use AI. It will become something that is more custom, and we will start seeing that shifts from very early on. When developers are start shaping their thinking, they will start understanding all these components.
turns.zh:
对我来说，我一次又一次地强调，Copilot只是个副驾驶，不是主驾驶。你仍然需要人工介入。但这意味着现在软件开发者或使用AI工具开发软件的人需要转变思维方式。首先，你需要开始更系统地思考，更注重架构设计。你需要思考如何利用这些AI工具助力自己取得成功？这不再只是编写代码的问题，而是要将思维提升到更宏观的层面，关注互联体验和互联系统。（08:36）：随着时间推移，我们会看到开发者们逐渐接受这种思维模式。诚然，如今我们在软件开发领域已能看到这种转变，但更多是在资深开发者中，而初级开发者则较少如此。初级开发者刚入行时，我们通常期望他们能编写简单的代码。（08:57）：但如果现在有AI助手帮助他们编写代码，他们就能从一开始就投入更多时间理解系统、理解所构建的环境或产品，而如今他们往往因忙于学习编程而无暇顾及。因此我认为这是一个关键因素。第二个我期待看到变化的领域是硬件开发，因为我们知道AI对资源需求巨大。
（09:24）：为了满足规模需求，我们需要提升硬件性能，优化CPU、GPU、计算能力和代码优化。这是另一个目前仅限于少数专家的领域，但我相信它将在软件开发全生命周期中变得更加普及。（09:44）：与AI的集成必将成为每个开发者的常态。如今我们已见证这种转变，开发者们开始接受AI工具，探索如何与AI融合，如何运用AI。这将成为个性化需求，相关转变从早期阶段就已显现。当开发者们开始重塑思维时，他们将逐渐理解所有这些组件。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I saw a stat that at Shopify over a million lines of code and their code base was written by Copilot, which I don't know if I can do the math, but I imagine that's more than one person would've written in their lifetime and probably many engineers write in their lifetime. And I think that number reminds us just how fast things are moving and how much is actually changing. (10:35): You also mentioned 92% of engineers are using AI tools already. Is there any other stats that you can share that might surprise people about the usage of Copilot, growth of Copilot, things along those lines?
turns.zh: 我看到一项数据，Shopify的代码库中有超过100万行代码是由Copilot编写的，我不知道能否准确计算，但我想这比一个人一生的编码量还要多，也许比许多工程师一生的编码量都多。这个数字提醒我们事物变化之快，以及实际发生的变革之巨。（10:35）：你还提到92%的工程师已经在使用AI工具。是否有其他数据能让人们对Copilot的使用情况、增长情况感到惊讶？

turns.speaker: Inbal Shani
turns.en: Yeah. Well, we have over 37,000 organization and more than 1.5 million developers that are using Copilot.
turns.zh: 是的。目前有超过37,000家组织和超过150万名开发者在使用Copilot。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow.
turns.zh: 哇。

turns.speaker: Inbal Shani
turns.en: And they're writing code based on our surveys 55% faster. Imagine that you can give a software developer even few minutes, half an hour back in every given day, how much more productive they're becoming, and also as a result, how much happier they're becoming. So we know that in a survey that we have run through our users is 85% of that participants felt more confident in their code quality and also code reviews were completed 15% faster without Copilot. And we know that usually no one likes to do code reviews. (11:32): So if we can help accelerate and make developers take their time in doing code reviews, and also if we think about removing frustration, then 88% felt less frustrated and more focused on their ability for coding. And that is just the beginning. We have different examples from our customers. I think Accenture is a recent one that we got where they had 88% of suggested code was retained. So we have a lot of these stats that are coming together to showcase the size and the impact of using Copilot and AI tools for software development.
turns.zh: 他们基于我们的调查编写代码的速度快了55%。想象一下，如果每天能为软件开发者多争取几分钟、半小时的宝贵时间，他们的生产力会提升多少，最终也会变得更加快乐。我们开展的用户调查显示，85%的参与者表示对自己的代码质量更有信心，而且在Copilot的帮助下，代码评审速度比未使用Copilot时快了15%。众所周知，人们通常不喜欢进行代码评审。（11:32）因此，如果我们能帮助开发者更高效地完成代码评审，并消除他们的挫败感，那么88%的人会感到压力减轻，专注力更强。这只是冰山一角。我们从客户那里收集了大量案例。例如，埃森哲（Accenture）近期案例显示，他们88%的建议代码都被保留了下来。这些数据共同展示了使用Copilot和AI工具进行软件开发的规模和影响力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Say companies hear these stats of like, oh, we're going to be 25% more efficient. Some people may think we need 25% less engineers. We're going to do all the same things. I imagine what you're actually finding is your engineers can do more. So it's not like you need to cut your people, it's that people can be faster and better.
turns.zh: 有些公司听到25%的效率提升数据后，可能会认为只需裁减25%的工程师。我们能否在不裁员的情况下提高效率？答案是肯定的。关键在于让工程师能更高效地完成工作。

turns.speaker: Inbal Shani
turns.en: No, let me be very clear, you cannot cut your people. You have to have a human in the loop. Copilot is a copilot, it is not a pilot. And I keep on saying that sentence again and again. I think the second thing that what companies need to realize, and that's another developer experience survey that we have run recently, that throughout the years we have added so much tasks on a single software developer from writing code, writing testing, interacting with people, collaborating with 21 people on every given week, going to meetings, waiting on builds, digging into legacy code, all of that is added to the fact that they need to write code, which is their basic work. (13:03): So most developers span less than 25, some say less than 20% of their time writing in code. So if we're able to give them half an hour back, one, they can write more code. Second, they can have a break and take a breath so we don't burn them out and they're more happy. Third, we give them more time for collaboration and creative thinking, so that sparks innovation. That is not something you want to cut back. (13:28): This is something you want to be able to give as a gift to your developers so they're happy with you and you can retain them. They can do their job. They're productive. Hence, they're happy.
turns.zh: 不，我要强调的是，绝不能裁减工程师。我们必须保留人工干预环节。Copilot是副驾驶，不是自动驾驶飞行员。这句话我反复强调过。另一项用户调查显示，多年来软件开发者承担的任务不断增加：写代码、进行测试、与团队沟通、每周与21人协作、参加会议、等待构建结果、处理遗留代码等，这些任务占据了他们本应专注于编码的宝贵时间。（13:03）因此，大多数开发者每天用于编码的时间不足25%，有些甚至不足20%。若能为他们赢回半小时时间，他们既能编写更多代码，又能休息调整，避免过度劳累，提升幸福感。第三，额外时间能促进协作和创新思维，这绝非可削减的资源。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I've talked to a bunch of engineers that use Copilot. One thing that surprised me is the most amazing engineers love Copilot. You think this would be for junior engineers learning to code better and faster, but 10X engineers say that... Someone told me it made them 50% better and faster too, which is incredible. What mistakes do you see product teams and engineering teams make when they rush to start adopting AI, integrate AI into their workflows?
turns.zh: 我与许多使用Copilot的工程师交流过。最令我惊讶的是，顶尖工程师也对Copilot赞不绝口。你可能以为这只适用于初级工程师，但10倍高手也称赞其效果显著。有人告诉我，使用Copilot后他们的效率提升了50%，这简直不可思议。当产品团队和工程团队急于采用AI并将其集成到工作流程中时，他们会犯哪些错误？

turns.speaker: Inbal Shani
turns.en: I think there are a couple things. The first one is companies expect a change to happen magically. Here's a tool, go use it. And it's not always flying the same way across all companies. So investing time in really taking the company through a change management process. The second thing that I'm seeing is that since AI is so hyped right now, there is often the questions of, oh, what should we do with AI? So there is that sense that I have to do something with AI. (14:38): Because if not, I'm not doing the right thing. Versus the question that for me is a big focus for my product team is, what is that problem that we're trying to solve and how can we leverage AI better to help solve the problem versus what do we do with AI? So it's really working backwards from the customer problem from what we're trying to solve, and then realize what are the best tools that we have in order to do that work better and think through that landscape versus, oh, AI is here, we have to use it. Because if not, we're not doing something right.
turns.zh: 我认为有几个方面。首先，公司期望变革能奇迹般发生。给个工具，就去用它。但这并不意味着所有公司都能顺利实施。因此，需要投入大量时间引导公司完成变革管理流程。其次，我发现由于当前AI热潮，人们常问："我们该如何应用AI？"这种紧迫感导致人们误以为必须采取行动，否则就是做错了。而我团队关注的重点是：我们要解决什么问题，如何更好地利用AI来解决问题，而不是简单地追问"AI有什么用"。这意味着要从客户需求出发，逆向思考如何用现有工具优化工作流程，而不是被动跟风采用AI技术。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there an example of that that comes to mind of someone that did that incorrectly or wasted a lot of time?
turns.zh: 你能举个例子，说明有人做得不正确或浪费了大量时间吗？

turns.speaker: Inbal Shani
turns.en: It's not necessarily examples, but I've been talking to some of our customers and they're coming to us. "We heard about AI. What do you think we should do with AI? And how should we adopt AI? And can we learn from your experience?" And I'm sharing our experience. When we started thinking about AI, it was with the idea to make developers much more productive. And what are some of the things that we've seen? That developers have multiple tasks on them and they don't have enough time to spend on coding. (15:45): So how can we give them time to spend more on coding and what are some of the coding element that we can automate? And from that comes the need to, okay, let's incorporate OpenAI, let's incorporate ChatGPT, let's connect all of them to help create that tool that helps developer be more productive and is AI based. So I'm sharing how we went through that journey to think about how to use AI. I see a lot of the times light bulbs with the customers like, "Oh, we didn't think about it like that." (16:15): It's more about we wanted to plaster AI on a lot of things versus I have this workflow and it requires a lot of manual work, or it requires a lot of configuration. Maybe I can think how to incorporate AI into that and really shorten the time or make it seamless or make it less friction for developers to adopt that tool and so on and so forth. So it's really sharing more how we are thinking about it and helping our customers to understand the same.
turns.zh: 倒不一定是具体案例，但我和一些客户交流时发现，他们常问："听说AI很火，我们该怎么应用？如何落地？能借鉴你们的经验吗？"我们会分享经验。最初考虑AI时，是为了提高开发者效率。通过观察发现，他们任务繁重，编码时间不足。（15:45）于是我们思考：如何腾出时间让开发者专注编码？哪些编码环节可自动化？由此引出整合OpenAI、ChatGPT等工具的需求，构建基于AI的生产力工具。我会分享我们的探索过程，常能激发客户灵感："原来还能这么想！"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Along the same lines, you're talking about how you think about it with your teams. It feels like your product teams are probably living in the future of how other product teams will operate because you have access to stuff everyone else doesn't necessarily have access to. They probably adopt these tools a lot faster than the other teams would. What are some ways that your product teams operate that other teams may not yet be operating?
turns.zh: 同样道理，你提到产品团队的思考方式。感觉你们的产品团队可能领先于其他团队的未来应用场景，因为你们能提前接触前沿技术，而其他团队尚未普及。能否分享产品团队的独特操作方式？

turns.speaker: Inbal Shani
turns.en: In GitHub in general, it's not just the product team. GitHub is GitHub. I'll say we eat our own dog food, and that means that we are the first to try every feature, every capability that we're developing. And it's not just our engineering team, it spans across GitHub. So for example, GitHub is running on GitHub. There are several blog posts and talks. Even in the recent Universe, we had a specific talk in terms of how GitHub is using GitHub and adopting AI across software development lifecycle. (17:32): And the biggest focus for us is if we're saying that GitHub is a developer platform and it's more than that, it's a software development platform, how are we making sure that all the persona that are taking part in the development of GitHub are also using GitHub? So for example, our finance team is using discussions and posts and PRs and reposts to communicate our AR numbers and so on and so forth. We have our legal team using, we have our HR team. If they like it or not, it's a different question. (18:02): But the idea is that we're using GitHub to run GitHub, and the product team is one of the first early adopters along with our engineering team. So for example, when we've tested chat and we wanted to see the quantity or the recommendation, the search, this is something that the product team was one of the first users to go and figure it out. Is it giving me the right thing that I need to do that? Is it summarizing the PR the way I want to summarize? And so on and so forth. (18:27): But we are really strong in advocating that we have to be the one testing our tools. If we cannot use them, our customers cannot use them for sure. So nothing is shipped before it spends enough months cooking inside GitHub, so we have to say this is working for us or not before we put it at the end of our customers.
turns.zh: 总的来说，在GitHub内部，不只是产品团队在使用我们的产品。GitHub就是GitHub。我想说我们自己也是产品的用户，这意味着我们是首批测试每项新功能、每项研发成果的团队。这种理念不仅限于工程团队，而是渗透到GitHub的各个层面。例如，GitHub本身就是在GitHub上运行的。我们有过多篇博文和演讲，甚至在最近的Universe大会上，我们专门做了一场关于GitHub如何在软件开发生命周期中应用AI的演讲。（17:32）对我们来说，最重要的关注点是——如果我们说GitHub是一个开发者平台，更确切地说是一个软件开发平台，那么我们如何确保所有参与GitHub开发的人员都能有效使用GitHub？例如，我们的财务团队正在使用讨论功能、发布动态、提交PR和转发内容来沟通我们的AR数据等信息。我们的法律团队也在使用这些功能，HR团队也是如此。至于他们是否喜欢使用这些工具则是另一回事了。（18:02）但核心理念是，我们用GitHub来运营GitHub，而产品团队与工程团队一同成为最早的尝鲜者。例如，当我们测试聊天功能时，想了解用户推荐量、搜索结果等数据时，产品团队是最先试用并验证这些功能的团队之一。我们会问：这个功能是否能满足我的需求？PR汇总是否符合我的预期？等等诸如此类的问题。（18:27）但我们始终坚信，必须亲自测试我们的工具。如果我们自己都无法正常使用，客户肯定也无法顺利应用。因此，任何新功能在正式发布前，都必须在GitHub内部经过数月的充分测试。只有当我们确信其稳定性和实用性，才会将其推送给用户。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: One of the magical elements of Copilot is how it just fades into the background. You don't have to chat with it. You don't have to tell it anything. It just infers, here's what you're doing, here's the answer for you. If you want to use, it's cool. If you don't, it's fine. Is there anything you could share about just the design philosophy of Copilot?
turns.zh: Copilot的神奇之处在于它能自然融入工作流程。你无需主动与它对话，也无需主动告知它任何信息。它会主动推断用户的操作意图，并提供对应的解决方案。用户想用就用，不想用也没关系。关于Copilot的设计理念，您能否分享一些见解？

turns.speaker: Inbal Shani
turns.en: Yeah. The design philosophy for Copilot is very much aligned with the working backwards concept that I just mentioned. It's really putting yourself in the shoes of your customers and figuring out what is it that they need, how is that experience going to work for them? If it's an extra tool and if you need to ask for it and if you need to ask for it or if you need to wait for it, then developers will not adopt it. (19:27): So because we developed it for ourselves first and we wanted to experiment with that, the design philosophy was put yourself in the shoes of a developer, how would you like that experience to be? In 2020, we had a group of GitHub engineers that were working with the design team and with OpenAI GPT to really figure out how we're going to build that and how it can work to help developers to do their job more efficiently, more productively, improve their collaboration and happiness, and so on and so forth. (19:57): But the grounding principle was the developer needs to want to use this tool. And the more you add friction, the more you add churn, the more you add complexity, the developers will not want to use their tool. We just talked about all the things that the developer needs to do in every given day. Now add to that mix, I need to learn how to adopt AI, we knew that it will not fly. So it has to be a seamlessly integration. It needs to be something that is very intuitive for developer to use to be successful.
turns.zh:
是的。Copilot的设计理念与我刚才提到的"倒推式思维"非常契合。它实际上就是要设身处地为客户着想，思考他们真正需要什么样的体验，如何才能让这种体验对他们真正有用？如果这只是一个额外的工具，需要手动启用、等待加载，那么开发者们是不会愿意采用它的。（19:27）正因为我们最初是为自己开发这个工具的，并希望通过实践来验证其价值，所以我们的设计理念是设身处地为开发者着想——他们希望得到怎样的体验？2020年，我们组建了一个团队，由GitHub的工程师与OpenAI GPT团队合作，共同探索如何构建这样的工具，以及如何通过它帮助开发者更高效、更富成效地开展工作，提升他们的协作效率和工作幸福感等。
（19:57）但核心原则始终是：开发者必须愿意使用这个工具。若增加操作门槛、增加学习成本、增加复杂度，那么开发者们就不会愿意采用它。我们已经讨论过开发者每天需要处理的各种任务。再叠加一项——我还得学习如何使用AI，这显然行不通。因此，必须实现无缝集成。界面必须足够直观，让开发者能够轻松上手并获得成功体验。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What are the success metrics for Copilot? It's such an interesting problem of measuring efficiency gains and productivity gains for engineers. What metrics do you focus on to tell you this is doing what we want it to be doing?
turns.zh: Copilot的成功标准是什么？如何衡量工程师的效率提升和生产力提升？你们关注哪些关键指标来判断它是否达到了预期效果？

turns.speaker: Inbal Shani
turns.en: We are in a world that there are no right metrics. There is no one metric to rule them all. It's a combination of the things that you're looking to measure out of adopting AI. You can think about measuring code quality using AI. Can you improve the code quality? Can you improve the security of your code by introducing, for example, our GitHub Advanced Security using AI? (21:00): So there's a lot of different metrics that if you combine them together are providing you with that developer productivity, and then there's developer productivity, developer collaboration, time gain, that if you're bringing them together are yielding the developer happiness. The biggest area of focus for us right now is the definition of productivity because we have so many users that are coming to GitHub and they're looking for that productivity gain. (21:27): But one of the things we're very conscious of as we continue evolving Copilot and AI across the software development lifecycle across all the tools, productivity is not the right metrics against each one of these components. When we're implementing AI to GitHub Advanced Security, writing more secure code is the right element. It's like how many secrets were we able to prevent from leaking? How many issues in the code we're able to detect and find and fix before you ship that? (21:51): So I think that the world of the metrics for AI is really a big one. We are working a lot with our customers as they're asking the same questions and they're running their own experiments within their companies to figure out what is it that they want to measure. The most easiest one is time, but time is, it's funny what I'm going to say, but time is not quantifiable as a success metrics because you can write really bad code really fast. (22:18): So it's really about how are we taking time and translating it to efficiency, to productivity, to something that are harder to measure, and then how does that lead to develop core happiness, which is another harder metrics to measure. So the combination of all these input metrics leading to eventually developer happiness is what we're focusing on.
turns.zh:
如今的世界并没有一个放之四海而皆准的衡量标准。衡量AI应用效果的指标并非千篇一律。这些指标应根据你希望达成的目标而定。例如，你可以考虑用AI来评估代码质量——能否提升代码质量？引入GitHub Advanced Security等AI工具能否增强代码安全性？（21:00）  
 实际上，诸多不同指标若能协同作用，就能提升开发者生产力。开发者生产力、协作效率、时间节省等综合效益，最终能转化为开发者幸福感。目前我们最关注的核心问题是如何定义生产力，因为众多用户使用GitHub时都期待获得生产力提升。（21:27）  
 然而，在将AI应用于GitHub Advanced Security时，衡量代码安全性才是关键指标。例如，我们成功阻止了多少机密信息泄露？在代码发布前检测并修复了多少漏洞？（21:51）  
 总之，AI衡量体系极为复杂。我们正与客户紧密合作，他们也在企业内部开展实验，以明确自身的衡量需求。最直观的指标是时间，但有趣的是，时间并不能直接作为成功标准——毕竟糟糕的代码可能编写得很快。（22:18）  
 关键在于如何将时间转化为效率、生产力等更难量化的指标，最终提升开发者幸福感——这才是更具挑战性的衡量目标。所有输入指标的协同作用，最终指向开发者幸福感的提升，这正是我们关注的核心。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, it's so interesting because engineers could end up spending more time coding because they're enjoying it more. They're getting more done. Also, more lines of code isn't a good metric because you don't want to know if those are good lines of code. That's a classic way to not measure engineers well. So to me, it feels like developer happiness is the ultimate metric. We had Nicole on the podcast who came up with this framework, DORA, that's an interesting way of just measuring developer experience, developer happiness.
turns.zh: 是啊，这真的很有趣，因为工程师可能会因为更享受编码过程而投入更多时间，他们能完成更多工作。不过，代码行数并不能作为衡量标准，因为你无法判断这些代码是否优质。这是衡量工程师表现的典型误区。在我看来，开发者幸福感才是终极衡量标准。我们请到的嘉宾Nicole提出的DORA框架，就是衡量开发者体验、开发者幸福感的有效方法。

turns.speaker: Inbal Shani
turns.en: Right. I think one of the things that we're talking to customers and we're trying to figure out how we're articulate is instead of time, can we talk about time to value? So from the moment you put a developer on a task, how long did it take you until you realize the full potential or the full value of that, if it's generating revenue, if it's in adoption, if it's time to market? You can define your time to value in different ways. (23:28): But eventually you're investing in AI tools to help your developer to be more productive, to be more efficient, to be more happy, and then is it impacting your time to value, which is something that's the business side that they're looking to measure.
turns.zh:
没错。我认为我们与客户沟通时需要明确的是：相较于时间，我们能否转换为价值实现时间？即从让开发者投入任务的那一刻起，到完全释放其潜力或创造价值（无论是创收、用户采纳，还是缩短上市时间）需要多长时间？你可以用不同方式定义价值实现时间。（23:28）  
 但最终，投资AI工具是为了提升开发者生产力、效率和幸福感，而这反过来又会影响价值实现时间——这正是商业层面最关注的衡量指标。

turns.en: How do you see all of that sort of thing playing into this? Do you see CEOs being like, "Here's the iPad app I want," I'm going to sketch it for you, and then just run it through Copilot version 10 and it writes it for you? I know that you're saying engineers won't be cut and only increase and become more efficient, but I guess where do you see that version of it going of just like, here's a sketch, build it for me?
turns.zh: 您如何看待所有这些技术与这项产品的结合？您是否认为CEO们会说：“这是我想要的iPad应用，”然后我会为您勾勒草图，再通过Copilot 10版进行生成？我知道您说工程师不会被取代，只会变得更高效，但您认为这种模式会如何发展——比如，提供一个草图，让它为您构建应用？

turns.speaker: Inbal Shani
turns.en: I'm thinking about that as a better collaboration tool versus a production tool. Because right now, a lot of the time where we see challenges in articulating ideas is the communication. It's the clarity of thoughts. So if we can leverage AI to improve collaboration, and you basically put a drawing in front of Copilot and it helps tell the story of what is it that you're asking your developers to do, it shortened a lot of cycles and the back and forth. So what did you mean? (25:53): Did you mean the button here, or did you wanted it pink, or did you want that application, or did you want that operating system? So if Copilot can help refine communication, and it's becoming likely the best collaboration tool that exists in the market, especially in the global world where we are where we see communication is ongoing challenges between different personas that are taking part in coming up with an idea and basically we see AI and in our view is Copilot becoming that next natural language conversation. (26:26): It's that translator that helps bring everyone on the same page because it's creating that universal conversation language, the same that math used to be.
turns.zh: 我认为这更像是一种更好的协作工具，而非生产工具。因为目前，我们在清晰传达想法时经常遇到挑战，关键在于沟通和思路的清晰度。如果我们能利用AI改善协作，让您把一张草图放在Copilot面前，它就能帮助您传达开发需求，这将大大缩短沟通周期和反复确认的时间。比如：“您是说这里的按钮吗？还是您想要粉色？还是想要那个应用？还是想要那个操作系统？”如果Copilot能帮助优化沟通，它很可能成为市场上最佳的协作工具，尤其是在全球化环境中，人们需要跨越不同角色之间的沟通障碍来构思创意。在我们看来，AI，尤其是Copilot，正成为下一代自然语言对话工具。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Reminds me, there's another conversation I was having with an engineer and he was saying how he loves writing those simple functions that Copilot is now doing for him and he's sad that it's doing it for him, but he doesn't turn that off. But he kind of is like, "That's what I really enjoy. These little things that I could just crack like sort function of some sort." I guess, is there anything you think we lose with so much of our code being written for us?
turns.zh: 这让我想起之前和一位工程师的对话。他说自己很喜欢写那些简单函数，而现在Copilot帮他写了这些，他虽然为此感到遗憾，但又不愿意关掉它。他还说：“这才是我真正享受的部分。那些小小的挑战，比如某种排序函数之类的。” 我觉得，当大部分代码都被自动生成时，开发者确实会失去一些乐趣。

turns.speaker: Inbal Shani
turns.en: I think each developer has their own part that they enjoy doing. And you don't have to use Copilot to write your simple code. You can use Copilot through a chat experience and use them as an AI assistant and brainstorm. We're giving you a set of tools, and we have a scenario in mind how you should use them. But what we're seeing is developers are using them very differently. Everyone is choosing their own flavor on how to use the tools. There is no right and wrong way to use it. (27:32): It's a tool. It's a language. When I was learning how to code, I used to code in C, and then Java became a thing. I'm like, oh, but this is taking away my job because I used to write all these functions and all these libraries and now Java has it all. And then Python came, which is another abstraction layer. It's like, okay, so now I don't even need to think about that because Python can do all of that. So it's a matter of how you use the tools and what you use them to do what. There are areas that I will still go and write in C, even today. (28:04): I don't trust someone inventing metrics for me in an efficient way if it needs to run on a very small CPU. So I'll do that myself. On the other hand, there is going to be an element that I'm going to delegate to a higher obstruction tool, and that's exactly the way I think about AI. You pick and choose how you want to use it. There is no global way that is the absolute truth that everyone has to follow. You need to think how you use your tools to do your job in a way that you're still keeping the things that make you happy. (28:34): On the other hand, use AI to do the things that you less enjoy. Maybe you like writing functions, but you don't like writing, testing, so generate unit testing and so on and let AI do its job for you and you still focus on the things you enjoy.
turns.zh: 我认为每个开发者都有自己喜欢的编码部分。使用Copilot来写简单代码并不是必须的。你可以通过聊天界面将Copilot当作AI助手，用它来头脑风暴。我们提供了工具，也设想了使用场景，但开发者们的实际使用方式千差万别。没有绝对正确的使用方式。（27:32）：这就是个工具。这是一门语言。我刚学编程时，用C语言，后来Java兴起。我想，天哪，这会抢走我的工作，因为我以前写过所有函数和库，现在Java都包办了。然后Python出现了，又是一层抽象。就好像，好吧，现在我甚至不需要考虑这些了，因为Python能处理所有这些。所以关键在于如何使用工具，以及用它们来做什么。有些领域我至今还会用C语言编写。（28:04）：如果要在极小型CPU上高效地实现某个指标，我不信任别人帮我发明出来。所以我自己动手。而有些部分，我会委托给更高层的工具，这就是我对AI的看法。你可以自由选择使用方式。没有放之四海而皆准的标准。你需要思考如何用工具完成工作，同时保留让你快乐的部分。（28:34）：另一方面，把不喜欢的任务交给AI。比如你喜欢写函数，但不喜欢测试，那就让AI生成单元测试，这样你就能专注于自己喜欢的工作了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Are you actually still finding time to code? Are you still writing some C on the side?
turns.zh: 你现在还有时间写代码吗？你还在业余时间写C语言吗？

turns.speaker: Inbal Shani
turns.en: A little bit now. Now I'm mainly playing with my older son, so he has more time to cook, but sometimes I enjoy spending time with him and brainstorming and talking about things and architecture. I think recently a few months back, he did a project on sensors and sensors integration, and he came across common filter, which was the thing that I used to do many, many years back. (29:16): And he's like, okay, what is it and how is it done? And then we went through that and I helped him think about the structure and the sensors fusion and all of that. And then sometimes I'm like, "Okay, move aside, here you go. This is how you..."
turns.zh: 现在偶尔会。现在我主要和大儿子玩，他有更多时间做饭，但有时我喜欢和他一起头脑风暴、讨论技术和架构。最近几个月，他做了一个传感器和传感器集成的项目，遇到了常见滤波器的问题，而这正是我多年前做过的。（29:16）：他问，嗯，这是什么？怎么实现的？然后我们一起研究，我帮他思考结构、传感器融合之类的。有时我会说，好的，你自己搞吧。这就是你该怎么做……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Turn on Copilot. Just kidding.
turns.zh: 开启Copilot。开玩笑的。

turns.speaker: Inbal Shani
turns.en: Mommy's Copilot.
turns.zh: 妈妈的Copilot。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's so funny. That reminds me, I was watching a talk of yours and you were training tuning models and LMS way back in the day, before it was very cool. And so you've been in this space for a long time. Looking back, is there something that you see now of where things were going that you didn't see at the time?
turns.zh: 太有趣了。这让我想起之前看你的一场演讲，当时你还在研究调优模型和LMS算法，那时候这类技术还不是很热门。你在这个领域深耕许久。回首往事，有没有哪些当下显而易见的趋势，是你当时未曾预见的？

turns.speaker: Inbal Shani
turns.en: I grew up in a world of niche AI where you have to be an expert and you need to be trained for years understanding how to tune a model, what is the right output, and you needed to understand how to build a simulation to test it, how to ingest data, focus on optimization. I've seen the evolution of AI throughout the year with all the talking devices and conversational AI, and then it started as a single term. It came up as a multi-term. (30:22): So I've started seeing that trend of more democratizing AI, but I didn't expect that boom of generative AI. Everyone that even doesn't even know what AI is, that they need to use AI. I think that was the thing that caught me by surprise because I was so trained that you have to be an expert to use AI. So for me that was aha moments, like hmm, this is interesting. So what's next?
turns.zh: 我在一个小众AI领域长大，那时你必须是专家，需经过多年培训才能理解如何调优模型、如何获得正确输出、如何搭建模拟环境进行测试、如何获取数据并专注于优化。我见证了AI技术的演进，从最初的单一术语到如今的多元化应用。（30:22）我逐渐注意到AI正变得更加普及，但没想到生成式AI会引发如此热潮。现在甚至连不了解AI的人都觉得必须用上它。这让我感到惊讶，因为我深知使用AI必须是专业人士。对我来说，这真是令人惊叹的时刻，心想：嗯，这很有趣。接下来会怎样？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you have an opinion on whether large language models are the end all and be all of where all this goes and just continue to add in compute and data? Or do you think there's another, I don't know, something on the horizon that's going to again completely transform the transformer model of AI?
turns.zh: 你对大语言模型是否是终极解决方案有何看法？是否认为它们就是AI的未来方向，未来只需不断增加算力和数据？还是说你认为另有新兴技术即将彻底重塑Transformer模型的AI范式？

turns.speaker: Inbal Shani
turns.en: I think we've pivoted very hard towards a generative AI and generalized AI can solve everything. I believe that the future is going back to scale back a bit to the niche AI. So we will live in a hybrid world where you still have specific AI models that are solving very specific problem where the generative AI will have its limitation. It's a general purpose tool, so it can be as good as the data sets, but it also try to find some statistical recommendation. Is it good? Is it not good? So it's limited by the training set that it has and it's trying to be everything for everyone. (31:43): There are going to be areas where you still need to train models. For example, I spend my time in the aerospace industry and in the automotive industry. I don't see self-driving car models that requires so much delicate, specific models, tuning, high safety regulation, all of that being developed on the ChatGPT. I might be wrong, but I think that eventually we will find ourself in the world of hybrid models and multi-models where there will be several LLM models coming together because each one of them will have their own benefit. (32:19): And then there's going to be a niche AI or a more configurable customized model for specific use cases. So that's my prediction of the future. But in 10 years from now, we'll all be smarter.
turns.zh: 我认为我们已经过度依赖生成式AI和通用AI，认为它们能解决一切问题。但我相信未来会回归小众AI。我们的世界将是混合型的，既有专门解决特定问题的AI模型，也有生成式AI的局限性。生成式AI是通用工具，效果取决于数据集质量，同时还试图进行统计推荐。但其局限性在于训练集规模，试图面面俱到。（31:43）仍有许多领域需要手动调优模型。例如，我在航空航天和汽车行业工作，我看不到自动驾驶汽车模型能在ChatGPT上开发出来。或许我错了，但我认为最终我们会看到多模型混合的未来——多个LLM模型相互协作，因为每个模型都有其独特优势。（32:19）同时，还会有针对特定用例的定制化模型。这就是我对未来的预测。但十年后，我们都会变得更聪明。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, the future hard to predict.
turns.zh: 是啊，未来确实难以预测。

turns.speaker: Inbal Shani
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I wanted to ask, so GitHub came up with this whole Copilot idea. We had Ryan on the podcast talking about how there's a researcher just experimenting with what can we do with a bunch of data. And then that essentially turned into, wow, this is actually working. Let's quickly scale this and launch it. (32:54): I guess is there anything you learned from that huge success within GitHub and Microsoft to find other big opportunities? Is there something you do about how you structure product teams or create space for people to experiment with things like this to find the next Copilot?
turns.zh: 我想问一下，GitHub推出Copilot这个项目的背景是怎样的？我们在播客中邀请了Ryan，他谈到有一位研究人员正在试验如何利用大量数据来实现某个功能。结果发现，这个想法确实有效，于是我们迅速将其规模化并推向市场。（32:54）：我想问，GitHub和微软在Copilot项目上取得巨大成功后，是否从中总结出其他重大机遇？比如在产品团队架构或为创新留出空间方面，你们有何经验？比如如何让团队有更多尝试新事物的空间，从而找到下一个Copilot？

turns.speaker: Inbal Shani
turns.en: It's a lot about that. It's a lot about creating that bandwidth for the team to innovate and experiment and carving that time out, but also being okay that not every experiment is going to be successful. So the shift to learn or to fail forward, these are the philosophies that I believe in. If you don't try, if you don't experiment, you will never innovate. And if you don't fail, you will never learn from your mistakes, you'll never learn from your experience, so you will not progress forward. (33:36): So really creating that ability to experiment, the same that we've done with Copilot or we've done in GitHub Advanced Security or even the way GitHub was created, it's all that innovative thinking that the teams have that are thinking about what is that next generation use case? What is the future developer will need to be happy, to be more productive, to do their job? In a world that software development is changing so fast, you have to create that bandwidth for the next generation, the next innovation. (34:08): And if you didn't have a chance to see that the two-day keynote in Universe, I highly recommend because we basically shared our next vision for Copilot with Copilot Workspace. We also had Satya Nadella on stage and he was very excited. He's like, "Oh my god, GitHub, if you build that, this is amazing." So you see that we keep on putting this vision forward again and again at least six months to a year before we even have something in the market because we're already thinking, we're already innovating, we're already on the next thing.
turns.zh: 这其中最重要的就是为团队创造创新和试验的空间，划分出专门的时间，同时坦然接受并非每次尝试都会成功。因此，学会从失败中吸取教训，勇于尝试和创新，这些都是我深信的理念。如果不去尝试，不去试验，就永远无法创新。如果不从失败中学习，就永远无法从错误中成长，无法积累经验，最终无法取得进步。（33:36）：所以说，创造试验的空间至关重要。正如我们在Copilot、GitHub Advanced Security，甚至GitHub本身的开发过程中所做的那样，团队始终保持着创新思维，不断思考下一代的使用场景：未来开发者需要什么才能更高效、更快乐地完成工作？在软件开发日新月异的时代，我们必须为下一代创新、下一代产品留出空间。（34:08）：如果您错过了在Universe举行的为期两天的主题演讲，我强烈推荐您去看看。我们在会上分享了Copilot Workspace的未来愿景，Satya Nadella也亲临现场。他激动地说：“天哪，GitHub，如果你们能实现这个功能，那简直太棒了。”正如您所见，我们会提前六个月到一年就开始规划下一个愿景，因为我们一直在思考、创新，始终紧跟技术前沿。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there something that you do to allow for that other than just these principles of ship to learn and it's okay to fail? Is there a way you structured teams or resource teams? Is it like you have a percentage of time to think about other ideas, or is it just generally we're okay failing, find time to work on other things?
turns.zh: 除了“先上线再学习”和“允许失败”的理念外，您还有哪些方法来支持团队创新？比如，您是如何组织团队资源的？是否有专门的创新时间段？还是说大家普遍认同“失败不可怕，关键是从中吸取教训”？

turns.speaker: Inbal Shani
turns.en: It's a couple things. One, it's spend time with customers and learn from your customers, because a lot of the innovative ideas are coming basically from conversation with customers because they're sharing with you their frustration, they're sharing with you what they would like to have, they're sharing with you what will be an amazing invention for them. So that's the first thing is creating that mechanisms. And we spend a lot of time talking to our customers and also talking to our community. (35:21): We're fortunate to be the home for all developers and home for all open source. Large open source foundation and small open source foundation are running on top of GitHub. So that's another feedback cycle that we have to really gather those ideas and those asks to help us shape the future. And then the second thing is really about the teams pitching idea. It's like, "I have this idea. I've been doing some research. Here's a paper that describes what is it that I want to do," and then we figure out, okay, when can we fund it? (35:49): How can we fund it? Can we allocate a specific bandwidth? Can we do a POC? Do we do that in that team? Do we do it as a V team? So we keep it flexible. And we also have a research team, which are GitHub vNext, that basically that's our day job is to think about the next big innovation. But in GitHub, innovation is coming from everywhere. It's coming from our field team that are talking to customers and are implementing different variations of GitHub for customers. And they'll come back with some feedback or an idea. (36:18): It's coming from the product team. It's coming from the design team, from the engineering team. It comes from everywhere. So if you try to structure innovation, you're losing that organic spark that is humanity. Imagine that someone say you have 15 minutes a day to be creative. I don't think it's the pull. So it's encouraging that thinking more than structured.
turns.zh: 这涉及几个方面。首先，是花时间与客户交流并向他们学习，因为许多创新想法都源于与客户的对话——他们会向你分享他们的挫折、愿望，以及对未来惊人发明的构想。因此，建立这样的沟通机制至关重要。我们花大量时间与客户沟通，同时也与社区保持互动。（35:21）：我们很幸运能成为所有开发者的家园，也是开源社区的归宿。大型开源基金会和小型开源项目都在GitHub上蓬勃发展。这为我们提供了另一个反馈循环，让我们能够收集这些想法和需求，共同塑造未来。第二点是团队提案环节。比如，“我有这个想法，我做了一些研究。这里有一篇论文描述了我的构想。”然后，我们会评估何时能为其提供资金支持？如何筹集资金？能否分配特定资源？能否进行概念验证？是在现有团队中推进，还是组建虚拟团队？我们保持灵活性。此外，我们还有一个研究团队——GitHub vNext，他们的核心任务是构思下一个重大创新。不过在GitHub，创新来自于方方面面——来自与客户交流并为其实现GitHub不同变体的现场团队，他们会反馈意见或提出想法；来自产品团队、设计团队和工程团队。创新若被条条框框束缚，就会失去人类独有的创造力。想象一下，如果每天只给你15分钟进行创意活动，我不认为这能激发真正的创造力。因此，我们更鼓励开放式思考而非刻板框架。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Can you talk more about that team that you mentioned? What is it called? The vNext team?
turns.zh: 能否详细介绍一下你提到的那个团队？叫什么名字？vNext团队？

turns.speaker: Inbal Shani
turns.en: The GitHub Next. Yes.
turns.zh: GitHub Next。是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Next team. Can you talk a bit more about what that team is and how that works?
turns.zh: Next团队。能否进一步说明这个团队的职责和运作方式？

turns.speaker: Inbal Shani
turns.en: They're basically applied scientists, research scientists that are working together, and they're really thinking about three, five years horizon. They're not thinking about the right now. They're thinking about what is the future for software development is going to look like. They're writing papers. They're running experiments. They're doing POCs. Their job is to invent the future. (37:16): But again, it's really a synergy because they're talking to the product, to their engineering, so they're getting ideas from that. They're talking to customers, or we're sharing feedback. So that's our GitHub Next. It's basically our research team.
turns.zh: 他们本质上是应用科学家、研究科学家，共同协作，着眼于三到五年的发展蓝图，而非眼前的需求。他们思考软件开发的未来趋势，撰写论文、开展实验、进行概念验证。他们的使命是开创未来。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And that's where Copilot emerged out of, is that right?
turns.zh: Copilot就是从这个团队中诞生的对吧？

turns.speaker: Inbal Shani
turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's so interesting because, I think I talked about this with Ryan, there's so many companies with a team like that. Like Facebook had a famous one, New Product Experience team. Google had Google... Forget what it was called. But none of them have really been successful is my understanding and this one was. Is there anything you think you're doing differently? Is it more science-based and research versus just product managers trying a bunch of different apps? I don't know, is there anything you think is key to this team being successful?
turns.zh: 这真的很有趣，因为我记得我和瑞安讨论过这个问题，有很多公司都有这样的团队。比如Facebook就有著名的"新产品体验团队"。谷歌也曾有过某个团队（我记不清名字了），但据我所知，这些团队都未能取得成功，而GitHub做到了。你们觉得自己做得不同的地方在哪里？是更注重科学研究而非产品经理去尝试各种应用吗？我不知道，你们觉得这个团队成功的关键因素是什么？

turns.speaker: Inbal Shani
turns.en: I think there are two elements for that. One is having the right people with the right mindset on the team, allowing them and giving them the bandwidth and freedom to innovate. And the second thing is that we're focusing on making things real. So we're not keeping them far or in disconnect from the product and engineering. (38:15): There's a lot of synergy, there is a lot of discussion, because what happens in teams that are not successful, at least from what I've seen, one, that the team is becoming basically an university, they write papers, but nothing is coming out of that, so nothing finds its well to production. So if you don't introduce that, how do we take it to production from day zero when you're thinking about a new idea? It's rarely that it'll go through that hump cycle and itself in production. And the second thing that companies tend to use these teams is too much tactical. (38:47): Here is that, "We need something in six month. Go invent it right now," and then they're basically creating another engineering or producting to think about the things that are now in horizon one. So I think in GitHub we found the right balance between having the right people, having the right mindset, but also creating that synergy between the future thinking to how we make it real, so we have a strong relationship, especially between the product team and GitHub Next, to make sure that this relationship are ongoing and ideas are flowing both ways.
turns.zh: 我认为有两个关键因素。首先，团队里要拥有具备正确思维模式的合适人才，同时赋予他们创新所需的资源和自由。其次，我们注重将创意落地。也就是说，我们不会让这些创意与产品和工程团队脱节。（38:15）：团队内部有很多协同效应和讨论机会。那些不成功的团队，至少从我观察到的案例来看，一是团队逐渐变成大学式研究机构，他们写论文但成果却无法转化为实际产品。那么如果不引入这种协同机制，当你萌生新想法时，如何从零开始将其推向生产阶段呢？很少有想法能在经过漫长周期后直接投入生产。二是很多公司对这些团队的定位过于战术化。（38:47）：比如“我们六个月内需要某个功能，现在就去研发吧”，结果这些团队往往只是为了应对眼前的问题而临时组建工程或产品团队，思考那些尚处在第一阶段的想法。因此，我认为GitHub在团队组建上找到了平衡：既有合适的人才和思维模式，又能在未来构想与实际落地之间形成协同效应。比如产品团队与GitHub Next之间保持紧密合作，确保这种双向交流和思想流动持续下去。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Today, you're chief product officer at GitHub, which is I think a dream job for a lot of people. Early product managers, senior product managers want to figure out how to get to a place that you're at today. And I'm curious what you found most helped you build the skills that were necessary to be successful in this role? Was it mentors, exec coaches, just doing the job for a long time? Anything else along those lines?
turns.zh: 如今你担任GitHub的首席产品官，这对许多人来说无疑是梦寐以求的职位。初级产品经理、资深产品经理都想知道如何能达到你如今的职位高度。我很好奇，帮助你建立成功所需技能的最有效方法是什么？是导师指导、高管辅导，还是长期积累的工作经验？还有其他方面的因素吗？

turns.speaker: Inbal Shani
turns.en: Combination. It's never one thing, because the role of the chief product officer is so broad. You're not just the head of products. And that's the mindset that is now evolving in the industry is that a chief product officer is more than just the head of product. They need to have a business thinking. They need to understand their go-to market strategy. They need to understand the sales play. They need to understand how engineering are building products. It's not just about let me write a set of requirements or think about the vision and the future. (40:16): It's how all these components in the company are operating together to build that product. And some of that you learned from looking into the leaders that you work for and see how they're thinking. From my first boss in the aerospace industry, I learned how to think system. Not to think just on the problem that I'm solving right now, but how the problem that I'm in charge in solving that filter that I'm responsible in tuning is connected to their control system and the ignition system and all of that and how is it eventually being displayed. (40:47): So that requires me to think from the get-go on the bigger solution, not just my component. So I think that's one. The second thing is really thinking about the people and change management and how you take people with you, because a product manager role is a very influential role and a lot of the things you do is influencing other people. Although everyone thinks that as a product manager you get to do things, you get to write papers, but you need to influence the engineering team to build a product that you want them to build. (41:17): You need to influence the revenue team to go with a go to market and sell the product the way you envision it. So there's a lot of influencing happening. You need to understand how to do that and building that skillset as a product manager from the get-go is very critical. So for me, it was the fact that I was fortunate enough to do different roles in the industry and learn from different people, but also looking up, looking across, and looking down into the people that I manage and what are the things I could learn from them? (41:47): What are some of the skills that they have that are not necessarily in my toolbox and how can I adopt them? What does success look like and what are some of the things that make people unhappy? And you don't necessarily want to have these tools in your toolbox. So it's a lot of what's yes and what's no in a combination.
turns.zh: 组合能力。这绝非单一职责，因为首席产品官的角色极为广泛。你不只是产品负责人。而当下行业正在形成的一种共识是，首席产品官的职责远不止于此。他们需要具备商业思维，理解市场拓展策略，掌握销售策略，了解工程团队如何开发产品。这不仅仅是编写需求文档或构思愿景与未来规划。（40:16）关键在于公司内所有部门如何协同合作，共同打造产品。部分经验来自观察你所效力的领导者，观察他们的思维模式。比如，我在航空航天领域的第一位上司教会我如何进行系统思考——不局限于眼前要解决的问题，而是要思考我负责调试的子系统如何与控制系统、点火系统等相连接，最终如何呈现成果。（40:47）这要求我从一开始就着眼于更宏大的解决方案，而非仅关注单个组件。第二点在于真正关注人才管理与变革管理，如何带领团队前行。因为产品经理角色极具影响力，许多工作都需要影响他人。尽管人们常认为产品经理只需撰写文档，但实际需要影响工程团队去构建你期望的产品，影响销售团队按照你的设想推广产品。因此，影响力至关重要。作为产品经理，从一开始就掌握这种影响力技巧至关重要。对我而言，得益于在行业中历任不同职位，向不同人学习，同时向上、向下、向内观察管理的团队，了解可以从他们身上汲取哪些技能。（41:17）比如，他们拥有哪些我尚未掌握的技能？如何借鉴这些技能？成功的标准是什么？哪些因素会导致团队不满？有些技能你可能并不想拥有。这就是组合能力中取舍的关键所在。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, it's exactly like you said, it's all the things combined. I really like that last point of just identifying people that are good at something that you want to get better at and just learning from them, watching them, maybe asking them questions about how they're operating. I am trying a new segment of this podcast called Failure Corner, and my question to you is, what's the biggest career or product failure of your career and what did you learn from that experience?
turns.zh: 是的，正如你所说，这是一系列能力的组合。我特别喜欢你最后提到的观点——识别那些在你想提升的领域表现出色的人，向他们学习、观察他们，或许还向他们请教操作方法。我正在尝试推出一个名为“失败角”的新播客环节。我的问题是，你职业生涯中最大的职业或产品失败经历是什么？从中你获得了哪些教训？

turns.speaker: Inbal Shani
turns.en: I'll call it the biggest learning because I'm not a believer in failure. I'm a believer in learnings. And every time you fail, it's a big learning and I prefer to look at that as opportunities. I think biggest one was likely early on when I started being a leader and the manager of a team, I'm a very go, go, go person and I have a lot of energy. And when I'm coming to something and I see all the issues that need to be fixed, it's like, okay, let's take the toolbox out. Let's go fix everything. And that includes driving change. (43:03): And I've seen that when I started doing that without building that understanding of why we need to do a change or why this is a problem that we need to go and fix it, then you don't take people with you through that journey. So really analyzing that not everyone appreciate change the way you are, not everyone has that mindset of the go, go, go, let's go do it. And really figuring out, taking a step back and assessing what is happening so you can take the team with you on that journey of changing. (43:35): That was for me, the biggest learning and likely a lot of the not supportive feedback I got from the team at that time was, "You're moving too fast. Slow down. Explain the why. Why are we doing that? How should we move forward?"
turns.zh: 我会把这称为最重要的经验教训，因为我不相信失败。我相信的是从失败中汲取教训。每次失败都是一次重大的学习机会，我更愿意将其视为机遇。我认为最重要的经验是在我刚开始担任领导者和团队管理者时获得的。我是一个行动力极强、精力充沛的人。当遇到需要解决的问题时，我总会想，好，拿出工具箱，开始修补一切。这也包括推动变革。（43:03）但我发现，如果在没有深入理解为何要变革、为何存在问题之前就急于行动，那么团队成员就难以跟随你踏上变革之旅。因此，我深刻意识到，并非每个人都像你一样看待变革，也并非每个人都具备那种积极进取、立即行动的心态。关键在于退后一步，评估现状，确保团队能与你同步完成变革之旅。（43:35）对我而言，这就是最重要的经验教训。当时团队给我的反馈大多是：“你进展太快了。放慢脚步吧。解释一下为什么要这么做？我们为什么要这样做？我们该如何推进？”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Where did this actually happen? Which company? Which role?
turns.zh: 这是在哪里发生的？哪家公司？哪个职位？

turns.speaker: Inbal Shani
turns.en: In TomTom when I was leading the location-based services team. And I think for me it was one, it was the first time I was working in international company, so really figure out that my character not always fly with every culture that exists. So how am I adjusting to that? And the second thing is that they were very accustomed in working in a specific environment in a specific way. And yes, I was hired to drive change, but one, the team doesn't have to accept. That's your job to drive change. (44:31): And also they're not necessarily on board with the fact that you're here to drive change. So how you take them with you through that journey was a big learning and being able to communicate in a general way of communicating to drive clarity, that was a big learning.
turns.zh: 是在TomTom公司，当时我负责定位服务团队。我认为对我来说，第一次在国际公司工作，让我深刻意识到自己的性格并不总能适应所有文化。因此，我需要调整自己以适应不同文化。第二点是，他们在特定环境中以特定方式工作已久。虽然我被聘来推动变革，但团队并不一定接受你的变革理念。这时如何让团队跟随你踏上变革之旅，就是一个重要的学习点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's actually a recurring theme on Failure Corner of the failure stories I'm thinking about is just somebody starting at a company and trying to change too much too quickly.
turns.zh: 这实际上是《失败角》节目中反复出现的主题，我所思考的失败案例中，很多都是新人加入公司后试图过快推动变革。

turns.speaker: Inbal Shani
turns.en: Right. It's very common because we are human beings. We think that if we're coming, we have our experience, we're coming to a new space, and you immediately see all the things that are not working or all the things that needs to be fixed. If you're working in the same space for a long time in the same team, you often don't see these gaps anymore because you got used to living with them. (45:15): So as someone new, you're coming in, you immediately see all these holes and cracks. And it's like, okay, here's all the things I need to fix. But you have a team that has been there for what? So how you find that bridge to communicate between the things you see and the things that they think is fine. Like, "Why are you driving these changes? It's be working. Don't fix it."
turns.zh: 没错。这很常见，因为我们都是普通人。当我们加入新公司时，凭借自身经验，认为自己能迅速适应新环境，但往往会发现许多亟待改进的问题。如果你在同一团队长期工作，久而久之就忽视了这些问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Inbal, is there anything else you'd like to share before we get to our very exciting lightning round?
turns.zh: Inbal，在我们进入激动人心的闪电问答环节之前，你还有什么想分享的吗？

turns.speaker: Inbal Shani
turns.en: For me, it's an exciting moment in time. I've been celebrating my first year in GitHub and my first GitHub Universe on stage last week. It was amazing experience for me to meet our customers, our partners and talk a lot about the importance of developer experience, our AI power platform, and how we're shaping the future. So I'm in a very exciting part of my journey with GitHub. (46:05): You don't get here if you don't make some mistakes and you do some learnings and you have some successes and then you take the right turn and sometimes you take the wrong turn, but you find your way to a place that makes you happy and feel fulfilled as a product leader.
turns.zh: 对我而言，这是一个激动人心的时刻。上周，我在GitHub Universe大会上庆祝了自己在GitHub工作的首个年头，并在台上发言。这次经历令人难忘，我得以与客户和合作伙伴交流，深入探讨开发者体验的重要性、我们的AI平台，以及我们如何共同开创未来。因此，我正处于与GitHub合作的激动人心的阶段。（46:05）：如果你不犯些错误、不断学习、取得成功、做出正确决策，有时甚至走错路，但最终能找到令自己快乐且充实的产品领导之路，那么你终将抵达成功彼岸。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. We're going to link to that talk in the show notes that people want to watch it. With that, we've reached a very exciting lightning round. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 太棒了。我们会在节目笔记中附上相关链接，方便大家观看。接下来是令人兴奋的闪电问答环节。准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Inbal Shani
turns.en: I'm ready.
turns.zh: 我准备好了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What are two or three books that you've recommended most to other people?
turns.zh: 你向他人推荐最多的三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Inbal Shani
turns.en: Failing Forward by John Maxwell, The Flywheel from Good to Great by Jim Collins, and a recent book that I read that is called Dare to Lead Like a Girl by Dalia Feldheim.
turns.zh: 约翰·麦克斯韦的《勇往直前》、吉姆·柯林斯的《从优秀到卓越》中的《飞轮》，以及我最近读的一本叫《像女孩一样敢于领导》的书，作者是达莉亚·费尔德海姆。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's a new mention on the show. Awesome. What is a favorite recent movie or TV show that you really enjoyed?
turns.zh: 这是节目中首次提及这本书。太棒了。你最近最喜欢的电影或电视剧是什么？

turns.speaker: Inbal Shani
turns.en: I like a lot of fantasy and I like a lot of history based movies and theories. There is a recent one that came up on Netflix, All the Light We Cannot See. Amazing. So well produced. Really tells an interesting part of the history of World War II.
turns.zh: 我喜欢很多奇幻题材和基于历史的电影及理论。网飞上最近上线的《我们所知道的世界》非常棒，制作精良，真实讲述了二战历史的精彩片段。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Have you seen Wheel of Time on Amazon Prime if you like fantasy?
turns.zh: 如果你喜欢奇幻题材，亚马逊Prime视频上的《时光之轮》你看过吗？

turns.speaker: Inbal Shani
turns.en: Yeah. Yes., I love that. It's done. It's a good one.
turns.zh: 看过。我超爱这个剧集。它已经完结了，很棒。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, especially season two is like wow. It's a lot better. Next question, do you have a favorite interview question you like to ask candidates when you're interviewing them?
turns.zh: 嗯，尤其是第二季，简直太棒了。比第一季好太多了。下一个问题：你在面试候选人时，最喜欢问他们哪个面试问题？

turns.speaker: Inbal Shani
turns.en: I think the first question that I really like to ask is, what is the most innovative thing you have done and why do you think it's innovative? And it's really interesting that there are some people that think they need to answer about the biggest invention that they've done, and there are some people that are very vulnerable and they talk about something very personal that they have innovated. (47:41): It shows a lot of their character. And I think the second question that I like to ask a lot is give me an example in a time where you had a disagreement with your manager, you're in the line with your manager, and then what did you do about it and how did you go? Because it showcase a lot about your character and are you willing to stand your ground and push up when you need to? And then what is that communication skills that you have, your influential skill that you have?
turns.zh: 我最喜欢问的第一个问题是：“你做过的最具创新性的事情是什么？为什么你认为它具有创新性？”有趣的是，有些人会说他们做过的最大发明，而有些人则非常坦诚，分享自己亲身经历的创新故事。这充分展现了他们的性格特质。第二个我常问的问题是：“请举例说明你与上司产生分歧时，如何与对方沟通，最终如何化解矛盾？”这个问题能很好地评估他们的沟通能力和影响力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you have a favorite life motto that you like to share with people, often come back to either in work or in life that you find useful?
turns.zh: 你有没有最喜欢的座右铭，经常在工作或生活中回味，并觉得很有用？

turns.speaker: Inbal Shani
turns.en: I think it's, if you don't take risks, you cannot create a future. I forgot who said it. I think it's from one of the animation Monkey Luffy if I remember. But it basically summarized the life motto that you have to take risks, you have to experiment. If you feel comfortable, it's not a good thing. You always need to feel uncomfortable to stretch yourself to go to the next thing. So that's something that I've done. You just heard about my career story from applied scientist to chief product officer. Who knew?
turns.zh: 我认为，如果你不冒险，就无法创造未来。我忘了是谁说过这句话。如果我没记错的话，这句话出自《海贼王》动画。但它本质上总结了一个生活信条：你必须敢于冒险，勇于尝试。如果你感到安逸，那可不是什么好事。只有当你感到不适时，才能突破自我，迈向新的境界。这就是我的人生经历。大家刚刚听到了我从应用科学家到首席产品官的职业转变之路——谁能想到呢？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that motto. lnbal, thank you so much for being here. Two final questions. Where can folks find you online if they want to reach out and follow up on anything? And then how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 我很喜欢这句话。Inbal，非常感谢你今天的到来。最后两个问题：如果人们想联系你或跟进相关事宜，可以在哪里找到你？听众又如何能为你提供帮助？

turns.speaker: Inbal Shani
turns.en: Lots of interesting sessions and talks from Universe. So if people want to learn more about what is it that we're doing, how we're thinking about AI, LinkedIn is likely the best social media platform to find me where I have a chance to talk to a lot of people. These are the best places.
turns.zh: Universe平台上有很多有趣的会议和演讲。如果大家想了解我们正在做什么、如何看待人工智能，LinkedIn可能是最佳社交平台，在那里我有机会与很多人交流。这些都是最佳渠道。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 听众又如何能为你提供帮助？

turns.speaker: Inbal Shani
turns.en: If you can share a similar experience or a story that you think will be helpful for me as I'm thinking about, what does that mean being chief product officer for GitHub, any tips and tricks on how you use GitHub, so maybe I can learn, or share your experience and story so I can learn from your experience as well.
turns.zh: 如果你能分享类似经历或故事，或许对我很有帮助。比如担任GitHub首席产品官意味着什么？有没有关于如何使用GitHub的技巧和窍门？这样我或许能从中学习，或者分享你的经验，让我也能从中获益。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. lnbal, thank you so much for being here.
turns.zh: 太棒了。Inbal，非常感谢你今天的到来。

turns.speaker: Inbal Shani
turns.en: Thank you so much for having me.
turns.zh: 非常感谢邀请我。

turns.zh: 再见，各位。非常感谢收听。如果你觉得这期节目有价值，可以在Apple Podcasts、Spotify或你喜欢的播客应用上订阅。也请考虑给我们评分或留下评论，这对其他听众找到播客非常有帮助。你可以在lennyspodcast.com上查看所有往期节目或了解更多信息。下期节目见。
